hints: Look at label X in Fig. 6.1 - it points to the dotted ring that sits between the viral envelope outside and the viral nucleic acid inside. What protein layer normally packages viral genetic material?
walkthrough:
Locate X in the diagram**
You are sitting with Fig. 6.1. Outside is the viral envelope with glycoproteins, inside is the viral nucleic acid. X is the beaded coat wrapped directly around that nucleic acid. That position tells you it is the inner structural protein.

Name the viral protein coat**
All viruses have nucleic acid surrounded by protein. That protein shell is called the capsid, made of subunits called capsomeres. So X is the capsid.
Final answer: capsid (protein coat / capsomere layer)

hints: Start by recalling what a healthy T-helper cell does after it is activated by antigen presentation - what chemical signal does it release to alert other lymphocytes?
Think about which two main lymphocyte types depend on that signal to divide: one that makes antibodies and one that kills infected cells. What happens if they are not stimulated?
Link fewer activated B and T cells to the overall outcome against any new pathogen - why would both antibody production and killing of infected cells fall?
walkthrough:
T-helper cells are the coordinators**
When a macrophage presents antigen, it activates T-helper cells. Activated T-helpers release cytokines, which are chemical messengers that stimulate other immune cells to divide by mitosis. If T-helpers are destroyed by HIV, this coordination is lost.

Humoral response collapses**
Normally cytokines stimulate B-lymphocytes to divide and differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete specific antibodies, plus memory B cells. With fewer T-helpers, fewer cytokines are released, so fewer plasma cells form and fewer antibodies are produced.

Cell-mediated response and phagocytosis collapse**
Cytokines also stimulate T-killer cells to divide to kill infected cells, and stimulate macrophages to become more active phagocytes and present more antigen. With fewer T-helpers, fewer T-killer cells are produced so less killing of infected cells occurs, and fewer macrophages are activated. Memory cell formation is also reduced, so secondary responses are weak.

Final answer: fewer cytokines released; fewer plasma cells so fewer antibodies produced; fewer macrophages stimulated / less antigen presentation and fewer T-killer cells stimulated to divide so less killing of infected cells / fewer memory cells produced

hints: Re-read the stem: both CD4 and CCR5 are necessary for the virus particle to enter. If the gene for CCR5 is mutated, what will happen to the shape of that coreceptor protein and its ability to bind HIV?
walkthrough:
Entry needs two locks**
HIV glycoprotein must bind to CD4 and then to the CCR5 coreceptor. Binding to both triggers the cell surface membrane to take the virus in by endocytosis.

Mutated CCR5 blocks entry**
A mutation changes the amino acid sequence and therefore the tertiary shape of CCR5. The viral glycoprotein no longer has a complementary shape to bind it, so endocytosis is not triggered and the virus cannot enter and infect the T-helper cell.
Final answer: virus cannot enter the T-helper cell as mutated CCR5 cannot trigger endocytosis / uptake of viral particle

hints: To make any antibody, you must first provoke an immune response in an animal. What would you inject into a mouse if you want anti-CCR5 antibodies?
After waiting for immunity, where do antibody-secreting B cells accumulate and how could you obtain cells that both make the right antibody and divide forever?
Think about the fusion partner for B cells and the final check - how do you keep only the cells making the wanted anti-CCR5 antibody for large-scale culture?
walkthrough:
Immunise with the antigen**
Inject a mouse with CCR5 protein as antigen. Over several weeks its immune system carries out clonal selection, producing B-lymphocytes and plasma cells that make anti-CCR5 antibodies.

Harvest B cells and create hybridomas**
Remove B-lymphocytes / plasma cells from the spleen. Fuse these cells with myeloma (cancer) cells to form hybridomas. This combines the useful properties of both: antibody production from the B cell and unlimited mitosis from the myeloma.

Screen and clone**
Screen the hybridomas to select only those producing the desired anti-CCR5 monoclonal antibody. Culture the selected clone in wells / fermenter for large-scale production of identical antibodies.

Final answer: inject small mammal / mouse with CCR5 antigen; immune response occurs; extract B-lymphocytes / plasma cells from spleen; fuse with myeloma / tumour cells to form hybridomas; screen / select for hybridomas producing desired anti-CCR5 monoclonal antibodies and culture on large scale
